#717. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

#716. Taylor Swift’s CMA Return Helped Disney Sell More Ads

Taylor Swift doesn’t work for the Walt Disney Company, but she may just have played a key role in helping the company carve out a little extra revenue.

Swift hasn’t performed on the Country Music Association Awards, televised on ABC, since 2013. On Friday, after the musician announced she would return to the program, Disney’s sales force opened some new streaming ad inventory tied to the event. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

“We were sold out.  We opened up additional opportunities because of Taylor, and we got additional interest, and we were seeing brands come in” all this week, says John Campbell, senior vice president of entertainment and streaming solutions at Disney Advertising, during a recent interview. “We can create demand 24 hours before the show.”

Such activity may be encouraging not only for Disney, but for the broader media sector, which is placing a growing emphasis on live events in a bid to keep the large audiences advertisers crave coming to its screens. Disney has in the last year put together a large schedule of sporting events and spectacles, including the CMAs, the College Football Playoffs, Dick Clark’s New Year’s Rockin’ Eve, the Grammys and the 2027 telecast of the Super Bowl — a string of big-ticket events that come with a large amount of advertising time that needs to be monetized.

Disney’s Campbell says ad revenue tied to the CMAs is up 20% compared to 2025’s telecast, and cites Madison Avenue’s desire for tentpole extravaganzas that are different from the rest of the TV schedule, as well as growing interest in creating bespoke promotions for social media and streaming video, along with traditional TV.

General Motors’ Chevrolet is returning for its tenth year as a presenting sponsor of the program. Its vehicles will be seen during the program, and country music artist Zach Top will appear in moments that celebrate country music and military service, among other things. Top will give fans a behind-the-scenes look at the creation of some of the vignettes he’s in via ABC and CMA social channels.

In a new venture, retailer Bed Bath & Bodyworks will be the presenting sponsor of live CMAs coverage on TikTok. Country star Lauren Alaina and digital creator Haley Baylee will serve up real-time content to fans, including branded moments, host integrations, interactive polls, and social engagement opportunities. “We know that fans want to interact with the show in so many different ways,” says Campbell, who notes this new type of sponsorship “provides additional content and more value for fans.”

Financial-services provider Ally is also new to the program’s ad roster. A new campaign will feature entrepreneur and reality show star Kristin Cavallari, and will surface during the show, on social and streaming venues and via linear TV commercials.

Advertisers interested in live specials are eager “to go beyond just the 30-second spot,” says Campbell. He believes new opportunities that weave marketing alongside musical content is driving “increases in overall commitments to our live specials.” There are, Disney no doubt hopes, a lot more to come.

Sufferin' succotash! The Monstars and Tune Squad interplanetary slam arrived 30 years ago, and it's still a clinic in interplanetary conflict resolution.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You just ordered a Pizza Hut and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew. You put on "Space Jam" to watch the greatest of all time team up with the Looney Tunes. It's a perfect evening… in 1996 or 2026.

The entire concept of "Space Jam" is so '90s that you swear you can hear Los Del Rio in the background mouthing, "Dale a tu cuerpo alegría, Macarena." As ridiculous as an intergalactic basketball match may sound, it's a perfect example of how even the strangest idea can work if you commit to it fully.

In case you thought you hallucinated the whole thing, no, you didn't, as the Looney Tunes find themselves in quite the predicament in this live-action-animation hybrid. A bunch of aliens known as the Nerdlucks arrive on Earth to abduct the Tunes and take them back as attractions to the outer-space amusement park known as Moron Mountain (shockingly nobody has claimed that subreddit, so do your thing, Internet!).

Being a wheeling-and-dealing wabbit, though, Bugs Bunny proposes a winner-takes-all basketball game between the Tunes and the tiny Nerdlucks. Unfortunately, the crafty aliens use their tech to steal the talent from ballers like Charles Barkley and Muggsy Bogues and turn themselves into the scary and skilled Monstars.

So, Bugs and friends reach out to Michael Jordan, who recently switched from basketball to baseball, to help the Tune Squad win this intergalactic b-ball matchup and their freedom, because if anybody can do it, Air Jordan (Hare Jordan?) can. Oh, Bill Murray also shows up here a few times. Why? Because he can!

"Space Jam" is a spin on the classic sci-fi trope of resolving high-stakes conflicts through sports. In 1975, "Death Race 2000" introduced a world where people drive like hooligans and bash into each other to get ahead and win races (ironically, this is the regular experience on any public road now). Meanwhile, in the same year, "Rollerball" demonstrated how to use extreme sports as a plot device whereby brutality trumped any kind of skill in the arena.

Yet "Space Jam" took this concept, cartoonified it for a family-friendly audience, and challenged the conflict resolution approaches of other alien invasion movies from 1996.

While "Independence Day" saw the heroes trying to destroy the mothership and "Mars Attacks" featured humans running away from "Ack! Ack"-ing extraterrestrials with ray guns, this film used the court to settle the score. It's an innovative way to deal with interplanetary matters, that's for sure.

Here's the thing: a basketball game is incredibly fair and puts everybody on equal footing. It isn't about who has the biggest guns or most high-tech spacecraft; it's about who can best work as a team to get a result.

Now, this isn't to say that the Looney Tunes and Nerdlucks ever planned on playing by the rules. Bugs challenged his opponents to a basketball contest because they were small and he knew the Tunes would have the height advantage. However, the aliens pulled a fast one by stealing b-ball talent and evolving into the brutish Monstars. Basically the cartoon version of when athletes use PEDs…

Even so, you can't argue that a basketball game gives each side a genuine chance at victory. Let's be real here for a moment: if humans were to face off against aliens in actual warfare, we would get smoked in seconds. Hell, we would probably get stuck in a tailspin of political infighting and the passing of the buck or end up destroying ourselves before the aliens even fired a single shot. On the court, though, there's no place to hide. Everybody needs to get up and slam!

There's also something magical about having MJ as the de facto leader of the Tune Squad. In the '90s, he was the closest thing to a real-life superhero that the world had ever seen. He broke basketball records, then headed off to another sport — baseball — to challenge himself. His love for the court never died, though, so he came back for the last dance. "Space Jam" found a clever way to blur the line between fiction and reality to elevate MJ's already iconic status.

Sure, Jordan wasn't exactly Daniel Day-Lewis in this film, but he did his best. "He did as well as he could do," director Joe Pytka told Entertainment Weekly. "He played himself, and remember, a lot of the film is based on his life, so there were realistic references there. He was very professional; he showed up, he knew his lines, and we made it as easy as possible.”

It's this type of dedication and professionalism that turned him into the greatest of all time. If you want to debate whether that honor belongs to LeBron James, go argue with a wall. We all watched LeBron in the 2021 sequel "Space Jam: A New Legacy," and let's just say that it makes "Morbius" look like "Casablanca" by comparison, and it deserves the flak it got.

Back with the infinitely better original "Space Jam" movie, it isn't just the courtside matchup to decide the Tunes' fate that surprises, but also the aftermath. Unlike other alien movies that see extraterrestrials being vaporized in the final act, this film demonstrates the power of humility in victory.

MJ understands that the Monstars only did the bidding of Mr. Swackhammer (voiced by the sensational Danny DeVito) and challenges them to free themselves. After the Monstars send Swackhammer packing to the moon, they befriend the Tunes, and there's good vibes all around. The beef is settled, and the only rivalry that remains is the competitive one on the court. That's all, folks!

Instead of treating the aliens as the enemy that must be destroyed, "Space Jam" looks at these creatures as misguided and simply following instructions. They aren't bad guys; they're foot soldiers. Once they break free from Swackhammer's shackles, everybody gets along. And hey, maybe Marvin the Martian also put in a good word for them.

It's a testament to the quality of "Space Jam" that everybody still talks about it 30 years later, but nobody can even remember Steven Spielberg's "Disclosure Day" from a few months ago.

In 1996, aliens were all the rage (and a little overexposed if we're being honest) but "Space Jam" still managed to find a unique and compelling angle that stood out from everything else around it. Not only that, but it also paid tribute to one of the greatest sportsmen to have ever walked the planet.

This wasn't just a slam dunk in cinema; it was boomshakalaka!

"Space Jam" is available to watch on HBO Max.

#714. Disney and AWS Team Up to Create AI-Powered ‘Star Wars’ Robots

The new creations, the Anzellans, will react to guests and each other in real-time, showcasing how AI could transform the theme park experience.

The Walt Disney Co. has hosted audio-animatronics at its theme parks going back to the opening of Walt Disney’s Enchanted Tiki Room in 1963. The decades since have seen presidents, beloved film characters and even Walt Disney himself turned into the audio-animatronics, relying on robots paired with scripted moments to complete the illusion for visitors.

But Disney and Amazon on Wednesday are pulling back the curtain on what Disney’s Imagineers think may be the next big thing in audio-animatronic technology: Robots with distinct personalities that can react to each other, and to visitors, powered by AI.

The audio-animatronic robots in question are The Anzellans: Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a, an alien species from the Star Wars galaxy that featured in the 2026 film The Mandalorian and Grogu that will make their public debut at Amazon re:Invent in Las vegas later this month. They were designed by Disney’s Imagineers, though they are powered by AWS.

“The work that we’re doing with Amazon dates back over a decade,” says Kyle Laughlin, senior VP, Walt Disney Imagineering R&D and Technology and Engineering, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “We’ve continued to work together in many different forums, everything from Disney+ to supporting Imagineering and the work that we do every day, and these three Anzellans from the Star Wars universe, originally in Solo, but most recently in Mandalorian and Grogu, are these incredible droidsmiths that we wanted to bring to life.”

The three robots each have cameras an microphones, with the AWS tech helping them determine what actions they take and alien phrases they should speak.

Samira Panah Bakhtiar, GM of Telco, Media & Entertainment, Games, Advertising and Sports for AWS, notes that the script and movements were all created by Imagineers, and the aliens don’t deviate from the movements and words written by the team, even if they use AI to help guide their actions.

“One of the things I’m most proud of at Amazon is how we obsess over making our customers successful and working backwards from their needs, and in this case, in this specific project, a group of AWS team members leveraged our coding tool called Kiro to be able to help take a lot of the ideas that the Imagineering team had and be able to help rapidly get it into a place where we could execute,” Bakhtiar says.

“I think that one of the unique things here is that each character is aware of three things happening at once,” she adds. “They’re aware of the guests in front of them, they’re aware of what’s happening in the workshop, and then they’re also perfectly aware of what the other characters are doing within the scene. And keeping track of all three of those at once really gives that experience that that they’re alive, and their reflexes and their judgments like all become part of that really unique guest experience.”

“I think what our guests you know are overwhelmingly saying all the time is that they want those character interactions that feel authentic and genuine, and as you mentioned, our audio animatronics today are very scripted in terms of how that interaction happens,” Laughlin adds. “When we launch with the Anzellans at [Amazon] re:Invent, it’ll be really the first time in which we will personalize that experience based on who that guest is.”

For now, the Anzellans will only be available to view at re:Invent, though it doesn’t take much to imagine that they will end up in the Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge worlds in California and Orlando eventually.

Still, the new robots demonstrate how Disney may ultimately use AI to improve its real-world experiences, while leaning into the creativity of humans in the process. After all, a visit to Galaxy’s Edge today will include actors dressed as characters, audio-animatronic robots, and even BDX droids, which are controlled by human operators.

“Ultimately the goal for Imagineering is to create a living world populated by all the characters you know and love,” Laughlin says. “Some of those are going to be audio-animatronics, some of those are going to be robots, some of those are going to be live performers, and some might be puppets. And I think our ability to blend all of those performances together is what makes us uniquely Disney and a one-of-one company in terms of delivering that kind of experience.”

EJAE is bringing her star power to Gap. The singer-songwriter behind Netflix’s blockbuster animated film “KPop Demon Hunters” is the face of GapStudio’s Winter 2026 campaign, showcasing a new 12-piece collection designed by Zac Posen.

Launching Nov. 20, the capsule marks the latest release from GapStudio, the retailer’s elevated fashion line overseen by Posen, Gap Inc.’s executive vice president and creative director. The new collection takes a more dressed-up approach to the brand’s signature American sportswear. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

Centered on a black palette, with accents of royal blue, deep red, winter white and neutral tones, you’ll find in the capsule denim, poplin and knitwear — this time with with sharper tailoring and exaggerated proportions. Standout pieces include a contoured rib maxi dress ($268), a structured denim jacket ($168), a denim double-breasted blazer ($198) and high-rise seamed stirrup jeans ($148).

One of the collection’s more playful designs is the Brannan Bear Sherpa Jacket ($268), a faux-fur outerwear piece complete with bear ears inspired by Gap’s longtime mascot.

“For Winter 2026, we wanted to move beyond traditional occasion wear with versatile pieces designed to be worn from day to night,” Posen said in a statement. “There’s still that level of drama with thoughtful tailoring and exaggerated lines, but it’s balanced by a focused palette that feels elegant and wearable.”

EJAE rose to international prominence as the singing voice of Rumi, the lead character in Netflix’s “KPop Demon Hunters,” and co-writer of the film’s breakout hit “Golden.” The song became a global chart phenomenon and earned the singer-songwriter a Golden Globe for best original song. Her appearance in the GapStudio campaign represents another crossover into fashion for the musician, who previously worked behind the scenes writing songs for K-pop acts including Red Velvet, aespa and Twice.

The release continues Posen’s efforts to elevate Gap’s fashion credentials through GapStudio, which launched as a more design-focused extension of the retailer’s everyday wardrobe. Earlier this fall, the brand unveiled a 20-piece collection modeled by Esther McGregor and Alton Mason.

The GapStudio Winter 2026 collection will be available beginning Nov. 20 on Gap.com and at select Gap stores, with prices ranging from $54 to $268.

#712. New York Knicks Star Josh Hart Inks Two-Book Deal With HarperCollins (Exclusive)

The NBA star will publish a memoir next year, and a children's book after that.

New York Knicks guard Josh Hart has inked a two-book deal with News Corp.’s HarperCollins, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

Hart will write a memoir, Live to Serve, which will be released in July of next year, and a children’s book, which will be released at a later date. The memoir will include Hart’s humor, faith, and heart, and will chronicle his college career at Villanova through this year’s NBA championship.

Senior VP & publisher Lisa Sharkey and senior VP & publisher Nancy Inteli negotiated U.S. and Commonwealth rights to the books with Anthony Mattero at CAA.

“I’m honored to be able to show readers how faith can shape the way they work, lead, compete, parent, and live their lives,” says Hart. “I’m writing for athletes and fans, but also for parents, coaches, young people, business leaders, and anyone who has felt overlooked or wondered whether the work happening outside the spotlight still matters. My faith journey means everything to me as a player, a parent, a husband, and a human and I’m excited to bring readers along with me so they too can Live to Serve.

“Josh Hart is the heartbeat of the New York Knicks. Whether he moves with the ball or without it, he serves his teammates and the greater good, and he gives glory to God first and foremost,” says Sharkey. “This book will inspire fans to learn more about Josh and will entertain them with his sense of humor, but most importantly, it will remind readers that on the court, a higher power always wins the game of life.”

“Josh brings the same incredible energy to storytelling that he brings to the court,” adds Inteli. “Like Josh himself, the picture book is full of warmth, humor, and especially heart. Families will want to read it again and again.”

A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth.

NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating."

During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1.

"This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4.

Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2.

A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet.

Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s.

The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did.

Voyager 1, meanwhile, took a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings, and the pre-biotic (pre-life chemistry) moon of its largest moon Titan, executing maneuvers which brought it high above the solar system's plane.

Hayes said the original design team likely did not foresee a 50-year lifespan for the mission, even though the Voyagers had many redundancies in them. But NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), which manages the mission, is looking to continue to max out the scientific return.

NASA says the mission costs from launch to Neptune, spanning about 12 years from 1977 to 1989, was $865 million — with $30 million more budgeted for its extended mission. "It's a lot of money, right? And it's everyone's money … so we want to make sure that we do it right," Hayes said.

Both nuclear-powered spacecraft are still healthy enough to be chatting with Earth and taking measurements from interstellar space, although dwindling power supplies have forced instrument shutoffs and other creative techniques to be getting the most out of the missions. One example was a huge power swap that took place on both spacecraft this year, called the "Big Bang" because of its impact on the mission.

"It's a balance, right? Because some instruments are more power hungry than others," Hayes said of the ongoing work on keeping the Voyagers going. "Those instruments that use the least amount of power, but give you good science still, they would obviously rise to the top in any sort of priority discussion. Whereas an instrument that is more power-hungry, but still has interesting science, that's on the cusp."

While the two spacecraft are still healthy, Hayes said their age — and the extreme environment they are operating in — makes them "fragile," in his words. "We're way out there. We're a light-day out there, which is just just over 16 billion miles. So it's really really far. It's also really really cold, right? We're only a few degrees above absolute zero here."

The Voyagers continue to lose four watts of power per year (their initial power was at 470 watts apiece) and the challenge is not only the power, but also the propellant. Hydrazine, Hayes said, is prone to freezing. "And if it freezes, then it's game over," he said, paying tribute to the JPL engineers that continue to keep the spacecraft going.

Voyager 1's next destination is vaguely near a star 17 light-years from our planet, in the constellation of Ursa Minor (the Little Bear, or Little Dipper). But the spacecraft will certainly be out of nuclear power by then, as its flyby — at a distance of 1.7 light-years of the star, called Gliese 445 — will take place in 40,000 years.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#710. Alix Earle Bares All: How the TikToker Is Becoming Beauty’s Next Billion-Dollar Mogul

She showed 8 million followers her flaws, then sold them the fix. Inside the 25-year-old’s sold-out, no-days-off skin care business.

Keeping up with Alix Earle is beyond the capacity of most mere mortals. Over the past year alone, Earle could be found delivering a perfect foxtrot on Dancing With the Stars weeks before shimmying alongside Pedro Pascal and Cardi B on Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl Halftime Show; vibing to Lady Gaga’s Coachella set and hours later lecturing a Harvard Business School class about the creator economy; falling in sky-high platforms at Kendall Jenner’s L.A. Halloween party, then strolling New York’s CFDA Awards red carpet (bruises hidden) in a gown styled by Law Roach. For weeks this summer, she cruised in a yacht along the Sardinia coast with Kylie Jenner BFF Stassie Karanikolaou, flying to Los Angeles for the Sept. 1 premiere of her Netflix reality series Earle Meets World (a global top 10 debut just renewed for a second season), all while weathering headlines about a rumored fling with Tom Brady and the messy fallout of a business rift with Call Her Daddy‘s Alex Cooper. Related Stories Lifestyle Oprah's Favorite Things 30th Anniversary List Includes Actor-Owned Apparel, Celeb-Approved Skin Care and More Lifestyle The 5 Best Red Light Therapy Panels for Improving Your Health At-Home

At the moment, though, seated in a sunny conference room inside Reale Actives’ Beverly Hills office, she’s taking her magnetic energy and putting it to work on keeping her winning streak alive.

Less than eight months ago, on March 31, Earle launched Reale Actives, a skin care brand formulated in collaboration with dermatologist Kiran Mian and tailored for sensitive and acne-prone skin. Developed in secret for two years, the four-product launch drew a record-breaking response from Earle’s online community — a fiercely supportive tribe, particularly after she shared a years-long, psychologically debilitating struggle with cystic acne. It generated $1 million in sales in less than five minutes. By midday, sales hit $5 million, and by 4 p.m., all products and sets had sold out completely.

It’s nearly lunchtime on a late-October day, and Earle, at the head of the table, is introducing five members of her team: CEO Andrea Blieden, director of influencer marketing and partnerships Katie Clementi, brand director Brianna Ellis-Mitchell, social director Logan Reynolds and, on Zoom, chief marketing officer Amanda Goetz. By year’s end, there will be 23 full-time employees across two office floors.

The brain trust is gathered to evaluate a top-secret item that will hit Reale Actives’ site in March to mark the brand’s one-year anniversary. Will it fit in with the rest of the product line, including the recently launched Go Calm serum? Is it giving REI? Does it need more branding? Maybe a free gift with purchase or a fun slogan? (“Zit girl” could work, but men buy the products, too, so maybe “dirty thoughts, clean skin”?) Do we like the shape?

Everyone weighs in. “Yes, I have my own opinions,” Earle says after the meeting ends, “but I trust their points of view. We all want the same thing: Everything we put our name on and ask our community to purchase with their hard-earned money must be the best product with the best quality.”

Blieden, whose résumé includes executive posts at Kiehl’s and The Body Shop, says Earle is totally dialed in and personally tests samples nonstop. “We have nine different text channels that include Alix,” she says. “She’s not like other celebrity or influencer founders. She is truly involved.” True to form, Earle connects directly with her consumers whenever she can. “I’ve seen her in every situation when people approach her, and she always stops to talk, introduce herself and get names. She gets addresses and sends product,” says the CEO. Once, when a user was having a hard time with breakouts, Earle had the company fly the fan to New York for a consultation with the Reale Actives dermatologist. All this while assiduously keeping up her prolific content creation, often with multiple posts daily. The day I visited, Earle posted a GRWM video that featured her putting on makeup and selecting an office fit for our interview: a gray cashmere sweater and pants, Saint Laurent Brigitte patent pumps and a Mombasa purse. It has since been viewed 1.3 million times.

“If you were to ask me, at any point before I was doing anything on social media, what I would want my career or end goal to be, I would have said having a brand of my own,” says Earle. “My dad and his brothers have a construction company together, and seeing how passionate they are about it has always been inspiring. I didn’t know exactly what kind of company I wanted or that it would come so early for me. The second I got this massive opportunity online, it was great — but I also understood that it can be fleeting. You have relevancy one moment, and it’s gone the next.”

Earle’s father, Thomas “TJ” Earle, says he never doubted his daughter’s ability to achieve a goal. “In her youth, she was a terrible basketball player, but she didn’t care. She was really small, but she went out there and gave it 100 percent. It didn’t matter that people thought she wasn’t good at it,” says TJ, who heads up Earle construction while managing the careers of Alix and her influencer sister, Ashtin. (Alix is repped by a powerful team that also includes senior agents at UTA and attorney Kevin Yorn.) “She did the same on TikTok. She was always giving the camera to somebody and asking them to take videos of her wherever we went. We all made fun of her and gave her the nickname ‘TikTok.’ She knew she wanted to do it and just kept powering through.”

TJ recalls Alix, while still in college, calling home excitedly to say that brands were offering her $250 for sponsored posts. These days, she reportedly commands between $250,000 and $500,000 per post for a one-off brand collab. While TJ won’t confirm exact figures, he says all her deals have one common denominator: “It always comes down to whether or not she truly likes it.” If she really likes it, he says she may “even do it for free.” Recently, Earle agreed to a deal to promote what she later said on TikTok was a foundation, but after trying the product, she realized she couldn’t in good faith endorse it. She told her agent to cancel the contract. “In some way, it feels so silly to be throwing away insane amounts of money,” she says, “but I really do just believe in longevity and maintaining that trust with my audience.” (Earle endorses and backs Cymbiotika supplements, GORGIE energy drink, SipMargs margaritas and was an early investor in Poppi, which sold to PepsiCo for $1.95 billion.)

Before launching Reale Actives, Earle fielded offers to become the face of several brands, deals that came with the freedom to claim she “did everything” to build it but meant she didn’t have to lift a finger beyond signing her checks. It never interested her. “This started as a concept in my head, and I want to be a part of every single little decision and detail,” Earle says. “The team does a great job of taking some of the front load off so that when we get in here, there are already different directions we can choose to go in.”

Earle does the hiring interviews herself. “The first two roles I interviewed were for a CEO and dermatologist. I’d just graduated college, so I was trying to find people who would share the same passion for the brand because I didn’t know how to rate their experience since I didn’t have any.” Blieden says she interviewed with Earle four times, put together a project presentation and underwent a surprise test. “It had come down to me and another candidate, and on a Saturday, Alix sent us each a text message that said, ‘Hey, I’ve been thinking about some stuff about the brand. Would love to discuss it with you,’ ” recalls Blieden. “I responded in 1.2 seconds because I was so excited. I guess the other person responded Monday.”

The hustle culture may not be for everyone, but there are no days off on social media. “She is lovely to work with, but she’s a beast and doesn’t mess around,” says the CEO. Adds TJ: “If you look at her calendar, it’s filled seven days a week, crisscrossing the country, meetings, events, photo shoots. Nobody could keep up with her pace. She’s just an animal.”

Earle describes scrapping the launch video they’d “spent so much time and budget on.” The clip was just “vibes,” nothing memorable. They jettisoned it for a nearly nude video featuring Earle dripping wet, unretouched — as all Reale Actives imagery has been since — to normalize imperfect skin. “I wanted people to think that two things can coexist: The line can be efficacious for your skin, but it can also be daring, fun and sexy. Skin care doesn’t have to be clinical and boring.”

The rollout ran on Earle’s knack for turning fans into co-conspirators, beginning with an Instagram account, @wtfisalixdoing, that dropped hints about the launch and continuing with influencers receiving locked suitcases containing a single puzzle piece, and a blank billboard in New York’s SoHo that put the pieces together one by one until the puzzle was completed, at which time creators received codes for unlocking the Reale Actives swag inside their suitcases. The award-winning campaign spanned a week, after having been fueled for weeks prior by Easter eggs on Earle’s social accounts.

Nick Brown, co-founder of venture capital firm Imaginary, which backs the brand and has also invested in Kim Kardashian’s Skims, Glossier, Farfetch and Tom Holland’s Bero, explains what has become known as “the Alix Earle Effect.” “You can count on a very small number of hands the number of times a creator has been able to move product at such a force that you start to realize it as an investor,” he says. “It’s seismic and not one-off. I kept seeing her do this — for mass brands, masstige brands, luxury brands, in beauty and in apparel. She really has a deep understanding for the brands she connects with and, more specifically, the connection between her own passion and what her audience will respond to. That’s why it’s organic and works so well.” Brands that enjoyed the boom included Giorgio Armani Beauty, Drunk Elephant, Patrick Ta Beauty, Charlotte Tilbury, Mielle Organics and NYX Makeup. Now that she’s applied her magic touch to Reale Actives, Brown confirms the business is already “very profitable” less than a year in and, he forecasts, is well on its way to becoming “a multi-hundred-million-dollar net revenue business.” Likening Reale Actives to Hailey Bieber’s Rhode and Selena Gomez’s Rare Beauty, he says, “She is constantly thinking about how to turn left, create an element of surprise and do something that’s a slightly different riff on what’s been done, enough to make people stop and say, ‘That was really cool.’ She is otherworldly when it comes to that.”

Despite what may seem like a charmed path to a reported $20 million net worth (so far), Earle has hit some speed bumps, facing criticism that it was her several rounds of Accutane, long considered a silver bullet, and not Reale Actives that cleared her skin. “I knew that was coming,” she says matter-of-factly. “But [the criticism] was not something I was afraid of because the truth is the truth. After I finished Accutane for the third time, my skin went back to being a mess and was probably worse than ever before. The moment that people started talking about it, I made a video and I showed my skin journey and was like, ‘Here’s before I did Accutane, here’s after I did Accutane, here’s before I started the products and here’s after I started the products.’ I have nothing to hide. I’m not lying. I actually use these products and nothing else.”

Earle also bore the brunt of the “negativity bandwagon” when she surfaced videos of her long (by American standards) European summer holiday. “Things got so negative this summer that it really helped me thicken my skin and gain a little bit more confidence in myself, knowing that you’re not going to be able to correct every narrative out there,” she says. “As a female founder, people want to put you into this box of ‘you can’t have.’ But you can let loose and have fun and share the human moments that we all have.”

Jumping from the phone screen to the small screen for Earle Meets World was also an adjustment. The series featured her divorced parents, TJ and Alisa Earle; her stepmom, Ashley (as in Dupré, the woman at the center of a 2008 sex scandal involving former New York Gov. Eliot Spitzer); four siblings and mom Alisa’s boyfriend, Todd. “I was worried going into it because I wasn’t sure if I would be able to connect with people in a different way than on socials,” she says. “But it gave people a completely different perspective on my life. As scary and embarrassing as those moments are, I really, really loved doing it.” Earle, who works with an acting coach, has passed on all scripts that have come her way, more out of fear of getting it wrong than anything else: “I only want to do something if it’s the right fit or I could be good at embodying that character.”

The season ended with Earle’s first on-camera comments about the falling-out with Cooper. Back in 2023, Earle and her podcast, Hot Mess, became the first creators signed to Cooper’s media network, Unwell. The deal lasted 18 months, at which point Earle found out she’d been dropped from Unwell when it broke in the media. “I constantly felt taken advantage of and used and mistreated and manipulated,” Earle said on her reality show, with her father adding that the podcast wasn’t given basic resources like video crews. Cooper has yet to comment on the drama.

Earle also recently faced a wave of criticism when she told a magazine that she’s never read a book. “Let’s clear the air: I have definitely read a book,” Earle tells me with a smile. “But no, I don’t actively read. I’m not reading anything right now.” (Other than — wink, wink — Daddy Issues, by Sofia Franklyn, who also had beef with Cooper; Earle posted a photo of herself perusing the title on TikTok overlayed with audio from Barstool Sports podcast hosts Dan Katz and Eric Sollenberger criticizing her admission. The clip had drawn 9.3 million views as of press time.)

A big teachable moment came in the form of her evolving relationship with her father as manager (dad-ager?): “She would not respond to emails, answer my calls or would roll her eyes at me in a meeting, which is typical stuff for a 20-something to do to their dad, but not someone you work with. Finally, I said, ‘Alix, listen, I’ve been doing this a long time with family, and here’s how it needs to work. There’s Dad, and then when it’s business, you treat me no differently than you would treat anybody else on the team.’ She’s super respectful to everyone, so that was easy for her.”

Running a business with multiple revenue streams and being smart about money were modeled by her dad, after all. She says, “I’m saving a lot, so some goes into a retirement fund, and I’ve invested in different stocks and bonds beyond the company investments. I always have the understanding that this can go away at any time, so I always keep that at the back of my mind.”

#709. DOC NYC Doc ‘Dryads,’ From Mallorca-Based Miguel Eeks, Explores ‘the Mystery of Creation Through Music’

Competing at prominent documentary fest DOC NYC, which also hosts its international premiere, Miguel Eek’s “Dryads” (“Dríades”) ponders the mystery of musical creation as he follows three indie musicians, Vasco Ribeiro from Portugal, Joana Gomila in Mallorca and Norway’s Emil Karlsen, as they source their music from their environs and local traditions.

Produced by Mallorca-based Mosaic, “Dryads” focuses on the creative process behind their works: Karlsen, a young Sámi musician and multi-instrumentalist, seeks inspiration for his joiks, the time-honored songs of his culture, in the fjords and tundra of northern Norway; Gomila explores the acoustic mysteries of caves, abandoned buildings and the expressive possibilities of the human voice, while Ribeiro, also known as Omiri, reworks traditional Portuguese music into something more modern and uniquely his own. Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

Despite their different approaches, all three share a common curiosity: how music comes into being, and how tradition, experimentation, improvisation and individual expression come together to create something new.

Through “Dryads,” Eek continues his exploration of observational cinema and its capacity to capture human experience through intimacy and shared time.

His most recent film, “Amílcar” premiered at IDFA, where it received the Outstanding Artistic Contribution Award in the Envision Competition.

He delved further into the making of his film with Variety:

You describe the act of making music as something almost mysterious. Did spending time with these musicians change the way you understand your own creative process as a filmmaker?

It was, in many ways, a journey of discovery. I wanted to explore the mystery of creation through music, which I have always considered perhaps the most mysterious of all art forms.

What I discovered, particularly through the time I spent with these musicians, was how many similarities there are between their creative processes and mine. Listening, for instance, is the first step towards creation. Joana, Emil and Vasco devote a great deal of time to inhabiting places, observing and listening to their surroundings, allowing landscapes and the people who inhabit them to offer clues about the music that will eventually emerge.

This made me realize that creation does not necessarily originate within ourselves. It also comes from what surrounds us, from our capacity to pay attention and to remain receptive to the world. I found many more parallels with my own experience of documentary filmmaking than I had anticipated.

All three musicians work outside the mainstream music industry, working with both inherited traditions and contemporary tools. Do you see their independence as an artistic choice, a necessity, or a way of resisting the increasingly standardized nature of the music business?

From the beginning, I wanted to explore forms of creation beyond the pressures of the music industry. I find it difficult to imagine these musicians preserving their freedom in terms of time, experimentation and working methods within increasingly standardized structures. Their independence is not simply an act of resistance; it allows a different approach to creation, rooted in craftsmanship, patience and a close relationship with their surroundings. For me, this is both a political and artistic choice: protecting the conditions in which something genuinely unexpected can emerge.

How do you balance observational intimacy and trust with the inevitable influence of the camera and filmmaking team on the creative process?

In ‘Dryads,’ I return to a working method developed in previous films, beginning with a pact of trust with the people I film. I then maintain a relatively static, unobtrusive presence. Over time, life and the creative process take over, and our small crew becomes part of the landscape. We never disappear completely, but we stop being a source of disturbance.

I don’t believe complete observational distance exists, nor should it be the goal. What matters is building a relationship in which the camera does not fundamentally alter the process being filmed. That is when a certain authenticity becomes possible, and the material that ultimately matters in the editing room begins to emerge.

The landscapes in ‘Dryads’ seem to become active participants in the creative process. Were you interested in exploring the idea that music is not simply created by individuals, but also emerges from a dialogue with place, memory and nature?

Absolutely. This is one of the central ideas of the film. We live in a time dominated by noise, haste, the constant distractions of our screens and a certain dehumanization of our relationship with the world. Through Emil, Vasco and Joana, I wanted to explore a less anthropocentric perspective, one grounded in listening and in a humbler relationship with our surroundings.

Nature and chance contribute something essential to the creative process that lies beyond our control and even beyond our understanding. The landscape is not simply a backdrop or a source of inspiration; it becomes an active presence, almost another collaborator. It can suggest, interrupt, transform and redirect the music. I find something reassuring in accepting that creation is not entirely under our control. Perhaps learning to surrender part of that control is precisely what allows something new to happen. Chance and uncertainty are essential to my work, as they are for many filmmakers who embrace nonfiction.

#708. A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability

"I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets.

But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic.

"In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule."

As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't."

Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions.

In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome, with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth.

Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility.

Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies. The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart.

"I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022.

The framework was crafted by King Charles III's Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI), which drew on the expertise of academics, heads of national space agencies and experts, such as Canadian astronaut and former International Space Station commander Chris Hadfield.

"It's like Stephen Hawking said, 'Stop looking at your shoes and look up'," Hadfield told Space.com. "It's really easy to spend a bunch of time on the news of the day, or the news of the week, or even the news of the month, you actually need something aspirational to be able to look up to some external measure of long-term success and goodness."

To Hadfield, the Astra Carta is an example of just that. It encourages humanity to embrace a global, peaceful outlook, which the astronaut believes will be vital to humanity's success as we venture deeper into space.

"If you view the moon as an eighth continent, which essentially it is, bigger than Africa, untapped, largely unsurveyed, whose laws are we going to follow as we begin to settle there?" continued Hadfield. "Or do we just transport kind of a silly imprint of our current geopolitics?"

The Astra Carta addresses a variety of interconnected challenges over its 33 pages and the 13 Articles of its "Zero Draft", which compliments and builds on the goals of existing treaties like the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, and the U.S. Artemis Accords.

Article 8 primarily focuses on orbital debris mitigation, and encourages the use of reusable launchers and responsible satellite disposal, investing in debris removal, and boosting public knowledge of the threat through education, among other measures.

But the Astra Carta's systemic approach reaches far beyond the threat posed by space debris. The remaining 12 articles highlight a latticework of forward thinking actions, ranging from the need for greater co-ordination between satellite operators to encouraging the development of novel propulsion and life support systems.It also calls for ethical guidelines on the use of AI in space, the establishing of key performance indicators for sustainability and legal frameworks for cybersecurity while advocating for treaties that prohibit the use of automated weapons in space, and so much more.

Each topic addressed in the Astra Carta looms large enough on its own. Taken together, they appear borderline insurmountable. But the convening power of King Charles III's SMI could prove to be a powerful factor in addressing them.

"What's interesting with the space economy is that the players within it are very fragmented, all over the world, and there isn't something that's sort of telling them what to do and how to behave in space," Sustainable Markets Initiative (SMI) CEO Jennifer Jordan-Saifi told Space.com. "And so there's definitely an appetite from all of those private sector players across the world … for something to galvanise common purpose."

To that end, the SMI has created a Space Sustainability Task Force to champion the principles of the Astra Carta, led by an advisory council that includes European Space Agency director Josef Aschbacher, UK Space Agency Director Paul Bate, Martinez and Hadfield.

The non-profit has advanced the goals of the Astra Carta at meetings of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space and by working with major players, including SpaceX. It also organizes high profile events such as the Nov. 7 Artemis Celebration Gala at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida, which honored Artemis II astronauts Reid Wiseman, Jeremy Hansen and Victor Glover while bringing together 450 leaders and pioneers from the space, government and business sectors.

In July earlier this year, His Majesty opened the UK Space and Defence Gateway at the Harwell Science and Innovation Campus in Oxfordshire, which partnered with the SMI and created an investment council to further the principles of the framework.

The Astra Carta's champions are actively engaging the private sector, governments and other luminaries. What's more, Jordan-Saifi believes that the voluntary nature of the Astra Carta could trigger widespread change faster than may be possible through the traditional U.N. system, which may need to be incorporated into country-level laws in a process that could take decades.

"The voluntary framework is the fastest way to get everyone on the same page. And then we might move to more concrete and enforceable, binding options in the future." In the meantime, Jordan-Saifi hopes that players in the space industry will play a role in holding one another accountable to observing the principles of the Astra Carta.

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

But could the competitive nature of the emerging space sector act as a barrier to embracing sustainability, as commercial entities race to capture their own share of the market?

"Space has become a very congested and competitive domain, and I don't, frankly, see the big players taking their foot off the gas, both for commercial and for strategic reasons," explained Martinez. "But I think that there is a growing awareness of the fragility of the space domain, and so, therefore, I would expect the major actors to recognise this and to behave responsibly."

Martinez points to SpaceX's Starlink constellation as an example of good behavior on orbit, with the company often sharing satellite trajectories and maneuver plans for other actors to see and plan for ahead of time. "...This is what I think we are all aspiring towards in the future, some form of global, globally coordinated, or global space traffic coordination system. which we don't yet have today."

A heightened risk comes from newcomers drawn to the growing space economy from other sectors. "They don't understand that they're entering a fragile and strategic domain, and that's where initiatives like the Astra Carta can help to socialise this awareness," continued Martinez.

But one of the greatest potential strengths of the Astra Carta may rest with its unique ability to engage the public and raise awareness in the quest for sustainability in space, as much as its capacity to galvanise the private sector.

"The first step is to create social awareness of this, and I would say that one of the values of the Astra Carta is the cachet of royal attention to this issue," said Martinez. "Extending the king's already well known appreciation for stewardship of the Earth environment to the orbital environment. And I think that is the real value of it … if the king is talking about this issue, [it] raises its salience and gets others to think about it."

In this, His Majesty is supported by the SMI and a team of astronaut ambassadors, including Hadfield, U.S. astronaut Nicole Stott and ESA astronaut Tim Peake.

"We're going to Antigua and Barbuda for the heads of government meeting of the Commonwealth, and the king attends that, and we're actually bringing Chris Hadfield on stage to talk to the 2.7 billion citizens of the Commonwealth about the AstraCarta," said Jordan-Saifi touting the SMI's ability to reach a vast global audience. "...We really want more and more people to be involved and be aware about space. And I think once people are aware of it, they want the same sustainability standards for protecting our planet."

However, the sheer scope of the Astra Carta makes it a challenge to communicate to the public. Potential readers may also be surprised to find that the most up-to-date version available on the SMI website is still the "Zero Draft" — the name commonly given to unpolished works not yet ready for publication.

Jordan-Saifi assured me that the Astra Carta's Zero Draft is still relevant and accurate, but that a version 1.0 is currently going through consultation for potential release in the future.

Which begs the question: how would one even gauge the success of so far reaching a roadmap as the Astra Carta? Its voluntary nature makes it inherently challenging, but as Jordan-Saifi notes, there are certain metrics that could be used to indicate how far the Astra Carta has shifted the space economy towards sustainability in the future.

The SMI could track the number of countries and commercial partners that have agreed to adhere to the principles of the Astra Carta, assess public awareness and gauge the success with which its tenants have been formally adopted by the United Nations and other regulatory bodies.

Hadfield, meanwhile, reflected on the difficulties facing the Astra Carta's champions on the long road to sustainability.

"How do you weave in the role of a space agency who has to answer to the national demands and the constraints that they have, both financially and politically?" questioned the former astronaut. "And how do you weave in all of the nonprofits that have all different agendas? The Astra Carta is trying to do all those things, and I think it's done admirably, but it takes patience. And if you're ready to declare anything after three years, you're making a mistake."

Want to know more? Then be sure to head over to the SMI website to read the Astra Carta in full, or you can read a recent op-ed on whether we are currently on track for true space sustainability.

Anthony Wood joined Space.com in April 2025 after contributing articles to outlets including IGN, New Atlas and Gizmodo. He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#707. UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists

A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.

Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

#706. Imax Promotes Giovanni Dolci to COO Amid C-Suite Moves

He fills the newly created role, while Mark Welton is upped to president, strategic partnerships as the film technologies company sees momentum from a Hollywood box office resurgence.

Imax has promoted Giovanni Dolci to the newly created role of chief operating officer, overseeing the company’s expanding global theater network.

Dolci, who joined Imax in 2012 and most recently served as chief commercial officer and executive vp, will relocate from London to New York City for his new role and report to Imax CEO Richard Gelfond. Building out its global theater footprint from beyond North America has long been a priority at the film technologies company as it rides momentum from having Chris Nolan’s The Odyssey and other Hollywood tentpoles popping at the box office.

“Imax is a stronger, more global business than ever, and we continue to evolve and grow our leadership team to capture the many opportunities ahead. Gio has a deep understanding of our business, our partners, and our people at every level. He’s been central to our growth for more than a decade, and his leadership will be critical in this next era of success for Imax,” Gelfond said in a statement.

Imax also promoted Mark Welton from president, Imax global theatres, to the new role of president, strategic partnerships, and also reporting to Gelfond.

Welton will lead partnerships beyond the company’s core theatrical business, working content programmers on new business opportunities across sports, events, and consumer brands. He has done earlier partnerships with the NHL, Major League Baseball and NBCUniversal, including the opening ceremony for the 2024 Paris Olympics.

“Mark has been instrumental in building Imax, and few people know our company and industry like he does. He is exactly the right person to turn the strength of our brand into new sources of growth,” Gelfond added.

#705. ‘GTA 6’ Earns Rave Reviews and Lands 99 Metacritic Score, Tying for Highest-Rated Game of All Time

The review embargo on “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally lifted and the game, which on Tuesday was nominated for Game of the Year ahead of its launch, is considered Rockstar Games’ latest masterpiece.

“GTA 6” currently holds a score of 99 on Metacritic, which ties it with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” for the highest-rated video game of all time on the platform. (The recently released remake of “Ocarina of Time” for Switch 2 has a score of 96 on Metacritic and is also a 2026 Game of the Year contender.) Related Stories Macaulay Culkin Returns as Kevin McCallister in McDonalds' 'Home Alone' Christmas Ad

“Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around ‘Grand Theft Auto VI‘ – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself,” Game Informer’s Matt Miller wrote in his review, which gave the game a perfect score of 10.

Thirteen years in the making, “GTA 6” is a massive open-world game that follows protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino (voiced by Manni L. Perez) who find themselves stuck in the midst of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida after a score goes wrong.

“Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series,” Luke Reilly wrote for IGN. “Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous ‘GTA’ games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it is invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.”

“GTA 6” costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version and reportedly offers approximately 80 hours of gameplay to complete its main storyline alone.

“I have quibbles about some clunky controls and some story pacing problems in the game’s later chapters, but like crappy cupholders in a million-dollar supercar, they don’t really get in the way of what’s here. Instead, they’re minor issues to point at as I hit the gas and go 200 MPH with the radio blasting,” Kotaku’s Zack Zwiezen wrote.

“GTA 6” officially launches Thursday in the U.S. but has begun rolling out worldwide as the clock strikes midnight on Nov. 19 in different territories, starting with New Zealand, which got access to the game Wednesday at 6 a.m. ET. While fans had been waiting to see if and when “GTA 6” reviews would drop before the game did (with several debating The Game Awards nominations being revealed before “GTA 6” was out), Rockstar Games chose to set the embargo in line with the game’s public release.
